Pass 2 adds Matt Hornbach (global head of macro strategy, Morgan Stanley; Sep 2025), John Normand (ex-JPM cross-asset strategy, now AustralianSuper; 2024), Jamie Patton (co-head of global rates, TCW; Sep 2024), Steve Eisman (The Big Short; Apr 2025) and Ashish Goyal (global macro PM; 2024), plus the hosts' own emergency episodes on the April 2025 tariff panic, the basis trade, Fed independence and the end of QT. One short from the culture-other cluster (GbZpAPJwCdY, on reserves and the 2019 repo spike) is borrowed for §7. Raw at _ingest/raw/2026-10-04/media/wall-street-skinny/. Seven cluster files had nothing on rates (a pay survey, a SPAC breakdown, a PE leverage episode, career shorts, an ad) and are only skimmed; seven pass-2 files added nothing new (listed under Gaps).

Time window: mostly April 2025 (tariff panic) to September 2026 (the first Warsh hike), with earlier anchors (the LIBOR end in July 2023, 2023 "101" episodes, Normand and Goyal in 2024, the Sep 2024 first cut). The transcripts follow one cycle all the way through, and that cycle is the note's spine: Powell cuts → Iran-war oil shock → chair transition → Bessent buybacks → hike. Dates are worked out from the episodes; figures are as stated on air.

Maps to: Course 11 (Global Strategy & Macro: this note is the rates layer the core-11 lesson points to but never builds), E9 (Geopolitics & Macro: the E9 lesson traces chokepoint → oil → inflation → rates → assets and then stops; this note picks up from "rates"), Course 02 (the 10-year is the risk-free input to every DCF), E2 (capital allocation: funding cost, duration of liabilities), Course 07 (reading probabilities off prices).

⚠ Bias: both hosts are ex-sell-side, and Jen's training shows. She is good on mechanics, quick to call something a crisis, and she labels her own speculation ("conspiracy corner"); the note keeps those labels. In April 2025 she calls herself the "leader of the panicking party," and the note airs Eisman's calm counter-case alongside. Two segments are paid ads (the Public.com bond account behind the 6.7% corporate-bond examples; Ground News), so read their framing as marketing even where the arithmetic is right. Medeiros works at a long-only asset manager and argued "not restrictive / sell bonds" consistently across both appearances. Hornbach runs sell-side strategy; Patton was long duration at TCW when she argued that cuts transmit weakly; Normand works for a pension fund and argues stay-invested. Burton runs strategy at a credit shop and argues that the risk is in PE, not credit. The hosts clearly admire Bessent and Warsh, so policy-maker motives get a charitable reading. Several stated figures are wrong or dated; each one is flagged where it appears.

What this adds to the program

  • A rates layer the repo did not have. GLOSSARY.md, learn/ and notes/ contain nothing on bond math, duration, the yield curve, the Fed's machinery or Treasury debt management. Core-11 teaches country risk and scenario planning, and E9 stops at "the Fed looks less likely to cut." This note supplies the next link in the chain: how a policy rate, a bond auction or a buyback reprices a mortgage, a corporate bond or a DCF.
  • The practitioner conversion factor. Bond P&L is duration × Δyield × notional, and desks size trades in DV01 (dollars per basis point), not in notional. With that one idea you can read every "macro fund blew up" headline.
  • Fed ≠ Treasury ≠ GSEs. There are three separate levers on long rates: Fed QE, Treasury buybacks and issuance mix, and Fannie/Freddie MBS buying. In 2026 they pointed in different directions. That split is the most useful framework in the cluster and the one the media got most wrong.
  • Reading probabilities off prices. The fed-funds-futures arithmetic behind "68% chance of a hike" is worked in full. It applies Course 07 and canon tetlock superforecasting to a market that sets the price of money.
  • The plumbing behind "the bond market broke." Cash vs. futures vs. swaps, why futures trade rich, how the basis trade levers that gap, why swap spreads are negative, and what LIBOR → SOFR changed (§10, §11). wss trading hedge funds covers the same basis trade from the fund seat.
  • Carry and tariffs as rate stories. The yen carry trade (§15) and the April 2025 episode in which tariffs made Treasuries, stocks and the dollar fall together (§16), with Eisman's counter-case.
  • A dated case study of institutional stress. It covers a chair transition, a criminal probe of a sitting chair, a hawkish appointee who surprised everyone, and the Taylor-rule framework for measuring "independence" with a number rather than adjectives.

1 · Bond price/yield and the yield stack

What it is. A bond is a loan. You pay a price today and receive fixed coupons plus principal later. The yield is the return those fixed cash flows imply at today's price, so when market yields rise the price of an existing bond falls, and the reverse. For a company, the yield it pays splits into two parts: a risk-free rate (the Treasury yield of the same maturity) plus a credit spread, which compensates the lender for the chance the company doesn't pay.

How it works. The hosts' figures (Public bond-account ad, 2024): a 5-year Treasury at 5% plus a 170bp spread gives a 6.7% corporate yield. Two separate things can make you money: - Rates rally: the risk-free part falls and every fixed-rate bond gains (sized in §2). - Spreads tighten: Treasuries stay at 5% but the spread compresses 170 → 150bp, so new bonds price at 6.5% and your locked-in 6.7% bond is worth more. You gain with no change in Fed policy.

The tariff short shows the other direction: Treasuries at 4% + 150bp = 5.5%, and tariffs widen the spread. The channel is covenants. With $400mm of debt and $100mm of EBITDA, leverage is 400/100 = 4.0×, inside a 6× maintenance covenant. If tariffs halve EBITDA to $50mm, leverage becomes 400/50 = 8.0× and the covenant is breached without borrowing another dollar.

Business significance. Every corporate borrowing decision reflects both legs. A CFO who watches only the Fed misses half the cost. In April 2025 Treasury yields fell (a flight to safety) while corporate all-in costs rose, because the spread leg widened more than the base leg fell. The hosts' summary: what's good for the US government is not necessarily good for companies.

Forces & impact. The base rate follows policy expectations, inflation and term premium (§3). The spread follows default risk, which is driven by input costs, demand, and how close covenants are to tripping. It also follows demand for income: in August 2025 IG spreads were at 30-year tights despite tariff uncertainty, and Jen calls it a "cash trap". With rate cuts priced in, few IPO exits, and equities "priced on the moon", money has nowhere to go except high-grade bonds, which compresses spreads. Second-order effect: tight spreads remove the cushion, so repricing comes "up by the stairs, down by the elevator shaft."

With vs. without. Without a separate credit spread, every borrower would pay the sovereign rate and lenders would have no price at which to take default risk. Credit would then be rationed by relationship, not price, which is roughly how bank lending worked before deep bond markets. When the mechanism breaks (spreads gap wider all at once), refinancing windows close, and the companies that most need to roll debt are shut out first.

Applies when / Breaks when. The decomposition holds whenever a liquid sovereign curve exists. It breaks when the "risk-free" leg itself carries risk (§6: the US is rated AA, below Microsoft and J&J, which the hosts point out), or when spreads are too tight to carry information. Burton's point is that OAS and the MOVE index can tell contradictory stories in the same week.

Channel example. Tariff Fallout: Why Are Credit Spreads Widening? (short); How Does Investing in Corporate Bonds Work? (short, ad); Chamath's New SPAC… The Fed vs. FOMC (Aug 2025, 30-year-tight spreads); Oracle CDS: the "Anti-AI Trade" (Nov 2025: Oracle CDS wider by ~95bp versus a modest move in CDX IG, which made Oracle the market's chosen hedge against AI).

Counterpoint. The 6.7%-yield examples are ad copy, and a 10-bond "IG and high-yield" basket is not risk-free carry. The covenant example assumes maintenance covenants. Much 2021–25 issuance was covenant-lite, which, as Medeiros notes, is itself a late-cycle sign.

2 · Duration, DV01 and convexity

What it is. If an oil stock rises 1%, you make 1%. Bonds don't work that way. Duration converts a change in yield into a percentage change in price; textbook-wise it is the weighted-average time to get your money back. A 10-year zero-coupon bond has duration 10. A 10-year coupon bond pays cash earlier, so its duration is lower (~8). DV01 ("dollar value of an 01") is the same idea in dollars: how much you make or lose per one-basis-point move. Convexity is the curvature that duration's straight line misses.

How it works. Rule of thumb: P&L ≈ −duration × Δyield × notional. - The blackjack-table framing (DV01 short): before you sit down you pick the $10 table or the $1,000 table. Duration is how a trader picks the table. A 10-year Treasury with a 5% semi-annual coupon has duration ~7.5 (a 10-year zero would be 10). On $100mm, a 1bp rally (5.00% → 4.99%) earns 7.5 × 0.0001 × $100mm = $75,000. - Sizing runs the formula backwards: a trader who wants "$100k per bp" buys $100,000 / (7.5 × 0.0001) = ~$133mm of 10s. Conviction is expressed in DV01; the notional is whatever falls out. - The issuer's side of the same number (Apr 2025): a $25B 10-year auction carries roughly $25B × 7.5 × 0.0001 = $18.75mm per bp. A 50bp backup into an auction is therefore close to $1B of extra present-value interest cost to the Treasury on one auction alone. - $1,000 corporate bond, duration 4.3 (Public ad): each 1bp move is worth 4.3bp of price, or $0.43 per $1,000. Yields fall 100bp (6.7% → 5.7%), so the gain ≈ 4.3 × 1.00% × $1,000 = $43, a little more in practice because of convexity. - Convexity, intuitively (Public ad, short): in the duration formula the yield sits in the denominator. When yields fall to 5.7%, you divide by a smaller number, so duration rises (say 4.3 → 4.4): you make money faster as rates rally. When yields rise, duration shrinks: you lose money more slowly. That curved price-yield line is positive convexity, and it is a property of option-free bonds. - A dealer's DV01 gone wrong (short, Feb–Mar 2020): a trader facilitated a client who sold $2.6B of long bonds, hedged by going short, and was then never delivered the bonds. The position carried ~$4.2mm DV01; as COVID hit, long bonds rallied ~50bp instead of selling off, and 4.2 × 50 ≈ $210mm, with the hosts putting the final loss near $250mm. A "flat" market maker can lose a quarter of a billion dollars when the risk it thought was hedged is not. - Iran war, March 2026, two traders each long $100mm (DV01 short): - 2-year: yield 3.40% → 4.00% (+60bp), duration 1.8 → 1.8 × 0.60% × $100mm ≈ −$1.1mm - 10-year: 3.96% → 4.45% (+~50bp), duration 8 → 8 × 0.50% × $100mm = −$4.0mm

The smaller yield move lost nearly 4× more money. This is why desks flip the question. They don't ask "how much did $100mm lose?" They ask "how many bonds give me $100k per bp?" A fund that wants "$1mm per bp" ends up with enormous notionals, and the hosts' tagline was that this is why the Iran war blew up macro funds.

Business significance. Duration is the unit of interest-rate risk on both sides of a balance sheet: a pension's liabilities, a bank's securities book (SVB's 2023 failure was a duration mismatch), an insurer's annuities, a homeowner's fixed mortgage. Matching DV01 is how a CFO hedges a planned bond issue. It is also how a "duration-weighted" curve trade (§3) becomes indifferent to the level of rates.

Forces & impact. Duration rises as coupon falls, maturity lengthens and yields drop, so low-rate eras manufacture duration risk. The 1.375% Aug-2050 Treasury issued in 2020 trades near 46 cents on the dollar (§9) because its duration was huge when rates rose 400bp. Second order: when everyone sizes in DV01, a vol spike forces simultaneous de-risking across funds.

With vs. without. Without a duration-type conversion, a "$100mm 2-year" and a "$100mm 10-year" look like the same risk. Sizing by notional systematically under-hedges long bonds and over-hedges short ones. Convexity is the tell when the approximation fails: mortgages have negative convexity (§12) because borrowers refinance when rates fall, so the holder's gains are capped while losses aren't.

Applies when / Breaks when. Duration works for small parallel moves in option-free bonds. It breaks for large moves (convexity dominates), for bonds with embedded options (callables, MBS), and for non-parallel curve moves, which is why §12 uses partial (key-rate) durations.

Channel example. Duration & DV01: the best explanation of the magic conversion factor (short, Mar 2026); What is "DV01" and how is it used? An intuitive explanation (short); Convexity Intuition Explained (short, Public ad); How do bonds work? (Public ad, 2024); Ferrari Loving Trader Cost Wall Street a Quarter Billion Dollars (short); It Wasn't Equity Turmoil That Spooked Trump (Apr 2025, auction DV01).

Counterpoint. The shorts loosely conflate modified duration and DV01. Strictly, DV01 = modified duration × price × 0.0001, a dollar figure, not a percentage; the futures video (§11) gets the Macaulay → modified → dollar sequence right. "Blew up because of duration" is also incomplete: the losses came from leverage on duration plus crowded curve positioning (§3). Likely error in the Ferrari short: it puts long-bond yields at ~3.72% in Feb 2020 falling to ~3.2%. The 30-year was nearer 2.0% → 1.2% over that window, so the bp move was larger than stated and the yield levels are wrong; the order of magnitude of the loss is still plausible. The auction "$1B" is a present-value cost to the issuer only if the Treasury could otherwise have sold at the pre-backup yield.

Links. canon taleb antifragile (convexity as the shape of payoffs; negative convexity = fragile) · canon perrow normal accidents (tightly coupled, uniformly sized risk) · Course 02 (discounting is the same math run in reverse).

3 · Yield curve, term premium, and curve trades

What it is. The yield curve plots yields from overnight to 30 years. Normally it slopes upward, because lending for longer means more opportunity cost, more inflation risk and (for non-sovereigns) more default risk. The extra yield for duration is the term premium. A curve trade bets on the shape of the curve rather than its level.

How it works. - Normal vs. inverted: 2s at 4.00% and 10s at 4.50% is a +50bp normal curve. 2s at 4.50% and 10s at 4.00% is a −50bp inversion. - Steepener: buy 2s, sell 10s, duration-weighted so a parallel move is P&L-neutral. You profit if the spread widens. A bull steepener comes from the front end rallying (the Fed cuts). A bear steepener comes from the long end selling off (fiscal or inflation fear). The flatteners are the mirror images. - 2025, US: after the "One Big Beautiful Bill", the curve steepened, but bull, with 2s falling on cut expectations, not 30s rising. Europe at the same time: the ECB cut ~8 times (~200bp total) and long-end Bund/OAT/Gilt yields rose, a bear steepener driven by term premium on fiscal expansion. The policy rate and the long end can move in opposite directions. - Sep 2024, the dovish cut that steepened the wrong way (Jamie Patton, TCW): pricing was split ~50/50 between 25 and 50bp; the Fed went 50 but the dots kept the total easing unchanged, only front-loaded. Faster-but-not-bigger easing should not rally the long end, so 2s rallied, 10s sold off (a bear steepener) and mortgage borrowers got nothing. - Sep 2025, carry as rent (Matt Hornbach, Morgan Stanley): the one thing to watch for the curve is the Fed, because cuts pull short rates down more than long rates. The 2025 steepening was a bull steepener on that pattern. Carry is "the rent you pay" to hold a position; a steepener is a negative-carry trade, so Morgan Stanley chose 3s/30s in Treasuries to keep the rent low (the SOFR swap version cost more, §10) and to avoid paying for timing it could not control. - Aug 2025, steepening from both ends: the attempt to fire Governor Cook produced a bull move at the front (more cuts) and a bear move at the long end (less discipline) at the same time. - 2026: "long steepeners" was the consensus trade going into the year. The curve had been a "Nike swoosh" (funds 3.50–3.75%, a dip to ~3⅜% at 2 years, then up). The March Iran-war oil shock turned one priced cut into ~two priced hikes and the curve bear-flattened globally, which "carted everybody out" (Jen); Caxton reportedly lost ~$1.3B on long-gilt steepeners. After the September Warsh hike the curve bear-flattened again: 2s and 5s rose, and 30s held.

Business significance. The Fed sets one point. Companies, homeowners and governments borrow everywhere else on the curve. Banks earn the slope, borrowing short and lending long, so a flattening curve hits bank equities even when the Fed hikes (Medeiros, Sep 2026). Issuers choose a tenor by reading the curve: term out when long rates are cheap, stay short when the curve is steep.

Forces & impact. The front end follows policy expectations. The long end follows growth, inflation expectations, term premium, supply, and credibility (§6). Medeiros's structural case for steepening is fiscal: public debt replaced private debt after 2008, so the private economy is less rate-sensitive (private debt-service ratios near 30-year lows) while the public balance sheet is more exposed. Global long ends are rising together. US 30s held above 5% for the longest stretch since 2007. German 30s underperformed US 30s over 12 months. Term premium rose most in the countries that cut most while inflation was still above target. Dutch pension reform removes a structural receiver of long-dated swaps, and the hosts cite an estimate of ~$20mm DV01 of effective paying as those positions unwind.

With vs. without. Without a term structure there is one price for all money, so a 30-year factory gets financed as if it were an overnight loan, and nobody is paid to hold duration. When the long end "comes unglued", as with Gilts in 2022 or US Treasuries in April 2025 ("essentially bidless for three or four weeks", Medeiros), mortgage rates, corporate long-bond costs and the government's own interest bill all reprice at once, whatever the central bank does.

Applies when / Breaks when. Curve trades work when the macro driver is identified correctly: a bull steepener needs cuts, a bear steepener needs a fiscal or inflation scare. They break on crowding. When everyone holds the same steepener, a labor-market surprise that prices out cuts bear-flattens the curve and stops everyone out at once (Medeiros's Jan 2026 warning, which came true in March).

Channel example. What is a yield curve steepener? (short); From Fixed Income Sales to the Buy Side feat. Jamie Patton (Sep 2024); Fixed Income Strategy 101 feat. Matt Hornbach (Sep 2025); Is This the End of the Federal Reserve? (Aug 2025); Chamath's New SPAC… Europe's Yield Curve Warning (Aug 2025); Head of US Macro at $1 Trillion Firm: 4 Forces… (Jan 2026); Wall Street is Watching Something More Concerning than Oil (Mar 2026); Why Stocks Could Drop 10% Before Year-End (Sep 2026).

Counterpoint. "Term premium" is model-dependent (ACM vs. Kim-Wright estimates differ) and is often used as a residual name for "whatever we can't explain." Medeiros's "countries that cut most saw the largest term-premium rise" is a correlation across a handful of countries, and fiscal expansion is a plausible common cause.

4 · The FOMC and market-implied rate odds

What it is. "Fed" is short for Federal Reserve, not an acronym. The acronym is FOMC, the Federal Open Market Committee, which votes by majority to set a target range for the overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to each other. The chair leads the messaging but has no veto. The fed funds futures market turns traders' bets on those votes into prices, and therefore into probabilities.

How it works. - Composition (as the hosts gave it): 12 voters out of 19 participants. The 7 Board governors serve 14-year terms, the chair (also a governor) a renewable 4-year term as chair, and regional bank presidents rotate in. The dot plot (Summary of Economic Projections) shows each participant's rate path anonymously. - Futures arithmetic (short, Sep 2026, target 3.50–3.75%, effective rate 3.63%, meeting on the 16th of a 30-day month): - The contract settles to the month's average effective rate, so implied rate = 100 − price = 100 − 96.29 = 3.71% - Known days: 16 at 3.63. Solve for the post-meeting rate: (30 × 3.71 − 16 × 3.63) / 14 = (111.30 − 58.08) / 14 = 3.80% - Expected change: 3.80 − 3.63 = 17bp; 17 / 25 = 68% odds of a 25bp hike - Year-end: the January contract (no meeting until late January, so it captures December's decision) implies 4.10%, and (4.10 − 3.63) / 0.25 = 1.88 hikes priced - Outcome: the FOMC hiked 25bp to 3.75–4.00%, unanimously. It was ~90% priced by meeting day after a hot CPI (Medeiros). - Who can be appointed, and why it matters (Aug 2025 emergency episode): all 12 regional presidents' 5-year terms expire together on Feb 28, 2026, and presidents need Board approval. Control a Board majority (Waller, Bowman, Miran in Kugler's seat, plus Cook's seat if she could be removed = 4 of 7) and you influence who the presidents are, and therefore the whole committee. - Reading the package, not the headline (Hornbach, Sep 2025 cut): the median dot moved to 75bp of 2025 cuts, a dovish first read, but only on a razor's edge; the only dissent was Miran (for 50), not Waller or Bowman. The SEP put Q4 unemployment at an average of 4.5% against 4.3% at the time, which implies a December print near 4.6%, yet showed only one 2026 cut. Hornbach found that hard to square. - Forward guidance trumps the move (Patton, Sep 2024): the market trades the Fed's action versus what was priced and the path the dots imply. A 50bp cut with unchanged total easing read as "bigger now, slower later." - Fed-day craft: desks diff the new statement against the old one word by word ("may" vs "will", where the comma sits), then trade the press conference separately; under Powell the two often gave opposite vibes (Hornbach, Jen).

Business significance. Every floating-rate borrower (SOFR loans, credit cards, leveraged loans) reprices off this rate. More important, the pricing tells you what is already in the market. A CFO deciding whether to lock a rate is trading against the futures-implied path, not against the headline. Two days before Warsh's first meeting, a 25bp hike was priced, so the move itself carried little information. The surprise was in the guidance (one more hike signaled, versus three priced).

Forces & impact. The dual mandate (maximum employment, ~2% inflation) drives the reaction function. Communication is a policy tool in its own right. Powell ran an open Fed, with dots, frequent speeches and public dissent. Jen argues this lowered event-day risk but added noise, because his press conferences sometimes contradicted the statement. Warsh wants the opposite: "do less", fewer forward-guidance crutches, disagreements settled behind closed doors before a unified statement. The second-order effect Jen derives from option pricing: if all information arrives on FOMC days, those days need higher event-day variance weighting in short-dated options. Medeiros (Sep 2026) adds that forward guidance is a zero-lower-bound tool and doesn't fit 3%-plus inflation, so front-end vol should rise structurally.

With vs. without. Without futures, "what's priced" is guesswork assembled from surveys and pundits. With them, any reader can extract a market probability in three lines of arithmetic. Without a committee structure, a single appointee could set rates, which is the fear behind the 2025–26 independence fight (§6). The committee is the main reason one dovish appointee (Miran) could only dissent, not cut.

Applies when / Breaks when. The arithmetic assumes 25bp increments, a stable effective rate inside the range, and no term or risk premium in the futures price. It breaks around liquidity events, when the effective rate drifts within the range (§7), and for far-dated contracts, where risk premia blur "expectation" into "price."

Counterpoint. Inconsistency across episodes: in one 2026 episode the hosts count 7 governors + 4 rotating presidents = 11. The Aug 2025 episode gets it right: the 12th voter is the New York Fed president, a permanent voter. That episode also says the dot plot projects "five years" out; it covers the current and next 2–3 year-ends plus a longer-run dot. The press's "most dissents since 1992" was disputed on air by the hosts themselves. And "68% chance" is a risk-neutral price, not a forecast. It embeds hedging demand, which is the gap between market odds and real odds that canon tetlock superforecasting warns about.

5 · Neutral rate, the Taylor rule, and financial conditions

What it is. The neutral rate (r*) is the policy rate that is "not too hot, not too cold". It keeps nominal growth stable with no inflation or employment pressure. Nobody observes it. The Taylor rule is a formula that outputs where policy "should" be from r*, the inflation gap and the unemployment gap. Financial conditions (stocks, credit spreads, the dollar, long yields) are the channel through which the policy rate reaches the real economy.

How it works. Medeiros's two cross-checks: - Jan 2026: the 10-year at ~4.15% versus Q3 nominal GDP growth of ~8%, nearly 300bp below. Borrowing costs far below the economy's nominal growth rate are not restrictive. Policy is loose. - Jan 2026, independence gauge: the policy rate was ~150bp below the Taylor rule, which is within history. The 1970s averaged 200–300bp below, and Japan in 2026 was ~200–250bp below. - Sep 2026: the gap had widened to ~200bp. Warsh said three times that financial conditions were too loose. Medeiros maps one more hike before year-end to 5–10% lower S&P, as conditions tighten to close the gap. - Nobody knows r*: in Sep 2024 the FOMC's longer-run dots ranged from 2.375% to 3.75%, with no more than three participants at any level. Patton's image: 19 pilots promising a soft landing who can't agree on the runway's elevation. - Hornbach's R − G rule for risk assets: in a Gordon-growth framing, the discount rate on future cash flows is the real rate minus growth expectations. If real rates rise and growth expectations rise by the same amount, the discount rate is unchanged and equities need not fall. In Sep 2025 real rates were inching down while growth expectations rose, which he offered as the reason stocks kept going up. - When cheap credit doesn't bite: Hornbach's formative read in Japan was Richard Koo's balance-sheet recession. Lowering the price of credit need not raise demand for it if borrowers are structurally insolvent and using cash flow to repay debt (Japanese corporates in the 1990s; US households after 2008). That view made him a long-running Treasury bull after the GFC. - Demand as evidence: record IG issuance at the tights and hyperscaler debt absorbed at higher yields means rates have not yet found the level that bites. Price discovery continues until demand breaks.

Business significance. "Rates are high" and "rates are restrictive" are different claims. A 4% 10-year with 8% nominal growth means revenue grows faster than funding costs, which is supportive of leverage, capex and equity multiples. Treating level as tightness was the 2023–25 consensus error behind the recession calls that "never happened" (Levine).

Forces & impact. Medeiros argues r* is higher than the 2010s because of fiscal deficits, AI capex, deregulation (~0.5% of GDP) and a labor force shrinking as immigration reverses. When policy stays below rule-implied levels, the short-run effect is good for stocks. The longer-run reflex runs through the long end and the dollar, "the relief valve", and then into inflation expectations.

With vs. without. Without a rule-based yardstick, "Fed independence" and "tight policy" remain adjectives argued along partisan lines. With one, you can rank countries by the gap and position accordingly. Medeiros's mentor's rule: buy the long end of central banks guarding against inflation, sell the long end of those that aren't.

Applies when / Breaks when. Useful as a gap signal, not a target. No central bank follows Taylor mechanically, and the output depends entirely on the r* you plug in. It breaks at structural breaks (pandemic labor data, supply shocks) where the output gap is mis-measured.

Channel example. Head of US Macro at $1 Trillion Firm (Jan 2026); Why Stocks Could Drop 10% Before Year-End (Sep 2026); Fixed Income Strategy 101 feat. Matt Hornbach (Sep 2025: R − G, Koo); From Fixed Income Sales to the Buy Side feat. Jamie Patton (Sep 2024: dot dispersion).

Counterpoint. Comparing the 10-year to one quarter of nominal GDP (8%, boosted by a post-shutdown rebound) flatters the "loose" case; trend nominal growth was closer to 5%. Medeiros was early. His Jan 2026 "neither cut nor hike" became a hike only after an oil shock he did not forecast. Burton's counter-view from April 2026 is that inflation would calm down after March. Hornbach admits the R − G rule cannot be tested: there is no time series of growth expectations, only his read of the room.

6 · Fed independence, the chair transition, and the "third mandate"

What it is. The Fed is designed to be insulated from the executive so it can raise rates when that is unpopular. The pressure point is the so-called third mandate. The Federal Reserve Act really does list three goals: maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates. Powell's reading (Sep 2025, via Hornbach) is that moderate long rates are the result of the first two, and Hornbach adds that "moderate" does not mean low. The political version reads it as keeping Treasury interest costs manageable. When that becomes the only mandate, monetary policy is being used to solve a fiscal problem (fiscal dominance).

How it works. The 2025–26 sequence as the transcripts record it: - Apr 2025: during the tariff panic Powell (Chicago, Apr 16) declines to offer a "Fed put"; Trump posts that Powell's "termination cannot come fast enough," the WSJ reports he is asking advisers about it, stocks fall back toward post-Liberation-Day lows and the dollar hits a 3-year low, and within a day the President walks it back. Jen's read: the market, not advisers, stayed his hand. Her line in the short: fire the chair and the "laws of physics" stop holding, so even a low policy rate won't produce low long rates once confidence in the bond market goes. - The independence argument is about perception (Aug 2025): if a governor can be removed on an accusation, every later decision is read as political whether or not it is. "Don't fight the Fed" only works when the Fed is believed; a Fed seen as captured invites the market to fight it. - Aug 2025: Governor Kugler resigns early, and Stephen Miran (a tariff theorist favoring lower rates) fills the seat through Jan 31 2026. The administration moves against Governor Lisa Cook over alleged mortgage fraud. The hosts note that she is a Biden appointee and that the press reads it as political. - Early 2026: the DOJ opens a criminal probe of Powell over Fed headquarters renovation costs. Senator Tillis blocks any nominee until it is dropped, and Murkowski and others back him. Medeiros reads this Congressional check as "the system working," and it made him less worried about the long end. - Powell's chair term ends May 15 2026, but his governor term runs to 2028. He chooses to stay as a governor, which is unprecedented in the modern era. - Kevin Warsh is confirmed. He is a 2006–11 governor, a balance-sheet hawk who opposed and then joined Bernanke's QE, and Druckenmiller-trained, as is Bessent. His agenda: steer with short rates, not the balance sheet ("indirect… hits financial instruments first"), keep the Fed out of fiscal policy, and run a unified, less talkative Fed. Jen's read: expect a cut-plus-steeper-curve regime. - Result: Warsh's first FOMC was hawkish, and he hiked in September 2026. Jen: "once and for all" this ended the sock-puppet narrative. - Why the third mandate tempts: on Jen's April 2025 numbers, a 25bp cut across the whole curve saves 0.25% × $9.1T = $22.8B/yr, and 100bp saves $91B, against a $1.8T deficit. The weighted average maturity of the debt is ~6 years, so short-rate cuts alone barely touch the bill. Long rates have to fall and stay down through a year of auctions.

Business significance. Credibility sets the long end, and the long end sets mortgage rates, corporate term funding and DCF discount rates. A central bank seen to be funding the government gets a lower front end and a higher long end plus a weaker currency, which is the worst mix for anyone borrowing long or importing.

Forces & impact. Debt (~$37T at the Warsh hearing, $40T crossed by Sep 2026, on the hosts' figures), an electorate that won't accept either tax rises or entitlement cuts, and midterms. Jen's own drift is the honest part. A rates purist all her career, she says aloud the US has "crossed the Rubicon", and asks how the debt gets financed without monetary policy. She offers a heroin/methadone analogy, and lists the tail options: "polite defaults", retroactive call features, the Fed buying directly at auction. The channel works through two of them in detail. An Odd Lots episode (Apr 2025) asked how ironclad Treasury documentation really is and floated a pen-stroke swap of all outstanding debt into 100-year paper; Jeffrey Gundlach's "polite default" (Mar 2026) would force-extend short debt to 30 years at the same coupon or cut coupons outright. Jen: "hard pass," because you get to break that glass exactly once, and then no one buys your next auction. Kristen maps it to private-equity liability-management exercises ("creditor-on-creditor violence," the Caesars restructuring).

With vs. without. With independence, the long end trusts that inflation will be fought, so the government borrows long at a modest term premium. Without it you get the 1970s template (policy 200–300bp below Taylor), currency weakness and inflation expectations that come loose, and Medeiros's rule says sell that country's long bonds. The "chairman's curse" episode is the market version of the same uncertainty: Greenspan (1987, Black Monday), Bernanke (2006, curve inverts on day one), Powell (Feb 2018, "Volmageddon" on his first day).

Applies when / Breaks when. Independence is protected by institutions (governor terms, a committee, Senate confirmation) only as long as Congress enforces them. It breaks when the confirmation process selects for loyalty, or when debt service crowds out other spending enough that markets expect accommodation regardless of who sits in the chair.

(short, Apr 2026); Every New Fed Chair Has Crashed the Market (Apr 30 2026); The truth behind the debt-refinancing theory (short, Apr 2025); New Fed Governor Miran (short, Aug 2025).

Counterpoint. The "chairman's curse" is three anecdotes with no base rate, and the hosts overstate it: on Black Monday the S&P fell ~20.5%, not "~26%" (the Dow fell 22.6%). Volmageddon was a short-vol ETP blowup (XIV), not caused by Powell. The $9.1T base in the refinancing math looks like the debt rolling within a year, not the total stock, so the savings arithmetic is narrower than "rates across the curve" implies. The ⚠ here is that the hosts' admiration for Warsh as a "serious person" is earned on his track record, but it is still a prior.

7 · QE vs. QT vs. reserve management: the balance sheet and its plumbing

What it is. Quantitative easing (QE) is the Fed buying long-dated Treasuries and MBS (and briefly corporate bonds in 2020) and paying with newly created bank reserves. It pushes long yields down and puts cash in banks' hands. Quantitative tightening (QT) lets those holdings mature without reinvestment. Reserve management purchases buy bills to keep reserves "ample" for the plumbing. They expand the balance sheet without targeting long rates.

How it works. - QE transmission (2008): the Fed cannot set mortgage rates. Mortgages have an expected life of ~5–7 years, so the Fed bought 5s, 7s and 10s (and 30s, "the whole curve") to pull down the risk-free rate off which mortgages price. Kristen explains why it's called "printing money": a dealer sells bonds to the Fed and finds new money in its account that didn't exist before. - QT and SOMA reinvestment (May 2025 short): QT allowed up to $25B/month of Treasury runoff, cut to $5B from April 2025. In a refunding month with $76B of SOMA Treasuries maturing, the Fed buying ~$71B at auction (e.g. $20B 3s, ~$15B 10s) is replacement, so the balance sheet still shrinks. The internet called it "secret QE." It was not. - Reserves (Aug 2025 short, borrowed): the balance sheet was down ~$2.5T from peak, almost all of it drained from the reverse repo facility. That left bank reserves (~$3.3T) as the system's buffer, with ~10% of GDP as a rough floor. Tax days drain reserves, and in Sep 2019 that produced the "repo spike": GC jumped from ~2–2.5% to ~6% in a day, "collapsed the basis trade" and, on the hosts' telling, created the Standing Repo Facility (see Counterpoint for the actual sequence). - Operation Twist (FX101 episode, Apr 2025): balance-sheet composition is a tool separate from size. By 2011 the Fed's QE holdings had aged toward the front end, so rather than grow the balance sheet it sold short-dated Treasuries and bought long-dated ones, about $667B in total (the maturity extension program), to push long yields down relative to short ones. Jen is candid that the later flattening and inversion had many causes besides Twist. - How QE actually happened on a desk: clients' offers were written on paper sheets before an 11am cutoff and run to whoever had a Fed terminal; the Fed picked levels. Always in the secondary market: the Fed cannot buy new-money debt directly from the Treasury, and it cannot forgive Treasury debt it holds. At auctions it only rolls maturing SOMA holdings (the "SOMA add-on" line in results). - Hornbach's critique (Sep 2025): the first QE rounds answered a deflationary shock, but the later rounds, including the maturity extension program, were spent chasing ~30bp of core-PCE shortfall (1.7% vs 2%). The mandate is stable prices, not exactly 2%, and he enjoyed a decade of predictable prices living in Japan. - Oct 29 2025: QT ends. Alongside a priced-in 25bp cut, the Fed ended runoff effective Dec 1, which Hornbach had told the hosts six weeks earlier it would not do. The tell was in funding markets: fed funds minus SOFR went from about −6/−7bp to about −30bp at October month-end, and standing repo usage rose. Agency MBS paydowns now roll into bills. Jen's second-order chain: Fed bill demand richens the front end, nudges the Treasury toward more bills and fewer 20s/30s, which also richens the long end and shortens the debt's maturity. "Not an Operation Twist, but a step in that direction." - Dec 2025: a 25bp cut plus reserve management purchases of bills through April. April is tax-day inflows to the TGA, and also Powell's last month as chair (Jen). - Medeiros: the Fed thinks ample reserves ≈ 10–12% of GDP; the balance sheet ≈ 25% of GDP. It is not technically QE, but "the balance sheet is not going down. So you can call it whatever you want."

Business significance. QE lowered every long-dated funding cost, including 2–3% mortgages, cheap LBO debt and zero-rate SPAC mania (Jen ties the 2020 SPAC boom to ZIRP). Reserve scarcity is a quieter risk. When repo spikes, every levered holder of Treasuries (hedge funds in the basis trade, dealers) faces margin calls at the same moment.

Forces & impact. QE is break-glass. Jen and Kristen argue that its normalization from 2008 onward, and its repetition in 2020, created both the 9% CPI print and the housing-affordability crisis (house prices roughly doubled 2018→2025 on their figures). Warsh's whole program is to stop using the balance sheet. Second order: a smaller-balance-sheet Fed leaves the long end to the market and the Treasury (§9), so expect a steeper curve and more term-premium volatility.

With vs. without. Without QE in 2008–09, the hosts concede, the bottom would have fallen out "into a depression and not a recession." With QE as a permanent tool, asset prices embed a central-bank put and inflation risk. Without ample reserves, the funding market seizes (2019). With permanently ample reserves, Medeiros warns, you have "created permissive [conditions] for risk."

Applies when / Breaks when. QE works when there is a disinflationary crisis and a transmission blockage. Using it during real inflation would be "pouring gasoline on the fire" (Jen, Mar 2026). Reserve management works as long as the Fed can find the scarcity point before it is hit. In 2019 it couldn't.

Channel example. Did the Fed secretly start QE again? (short, May 2025); The Fed: is this new QE? (short, Dec 2025); Who controls mortgage rates? (short, Mar 2026); The potential financial crisis that no one is talking about (short, Aug 2025, culture-other cluster); FX101, Operation Twist and Yale's $6bn Sale (Apr 2025); Meta & xAI as Project Finance 101 PLUS… the Fed's Insane Press Conference (Oct 31 2025, end of QT); Fixed Income Strategy 101 feat. Matt Hornbach (Sep 2025); Wall Street is Watching Something More Concerning than Oil (Mar 2026, open market operations and SOMA add-ons).

Counterpoint. "QE caused 9% inflation" overstates it. 2021–22 also had fiscal transfers, supply shocks and energy. Japan ran QE for two decades without that outcome, though Burton's answer is that "the US is not Japan." The hosts' 2019 numbers are approximate: SOFR printed ~5.25% with intraday GC trades near 10%. Jen also admits on air that her Aug-2025 "precipice of crisis" call was dramatic, and that the Fed simply ended QT. Sequence error: in 2019 the Fed responded with temporary repo operations and bill purchases; the Standing Repo Facility was created in July 2021. The Aug 2025 episode also puts interest on reserves at the floor; it is set inside the range, with the reverse repo rate at the bottom. Hornbach's "QT won't end this year" call (Sep 2025) was wrong within six weeks, a reminder that even the most senior strategist's balance-sheet forecasts are guesses about a committee. The Oct 2025 episode implies runoff was MBS-only; Treasury runoff (capped at $5B/month) ended too.

8 · Treasury auctions and who buys the debt

What it is. The US Treasury sells debt on a published calendar: bills weekly, 2s/3s/5s/7s monthly, and new 10s, 20s and 30s quarterly at the refunding (February, May, August, November) with smaller reopenings in the following months. Auctions are single-price ("Dutch"): everyone pays the yield at which the last dollar clears.

How it works. - Bonds trade before they exist as when-issued (WI) securities, quoted as a spread to the current on-the-run, so traders can price the "roll". - Bidders: direct (an account with the Treasury), indirect (bidding through a primary dealer or, in practice, the NY Fed), and dealers, who are obliged to bid. Competitive bids are capped at 35% of the auction and non-competitive bids at $10mm (retail). - Example: $25B 10s are offered, and the yield on the 25-billionth dollar is the clearing level for all. Results come out just after 1:00pm. Clearing above the 1pm WI yield is a tail (weak), at it is on the screws, below it means it stopped through (strong). - Pricing the WI (Mar 2026 episode): with the on-the-run 5-year at 4.00%, the new 5-year adds a month of term premium plus a supply concession, worth ~1bp, so the WI trades at 4.01%. Clearing at 3.99 is a 2bp stop-through; 4.01 is on the screws; 4.03 is a 2bp tail. Context matters: a 2bp stop-through after a 10bp pre-auction concession is not strong. Primary dealers must bid, so a high dealer takedown means end demand was missing; dealers then "puke" the paper into the market. - April 2025 sequence (Apr 11 episode): the 10-year went from ~3.9% after Liberation Day to ~4.5%. The 3-year tailed ~2.5–3bp with the lowest direct share since COVID. The 10-year cheapened 18bp into its auction, stopped through, but showed 1.4% direct versus a ~17.5% recent average. Ten minutes later the 90-day tariff pause was announced. The 30-year the next day drew ~30% direct, which Jen read as the world signalling approval. Her frame: foreigners hold ~25–30% of US debt and can "vote with their wallets" at auction. - March 2026, the front end: 2s, 5s and 7s all tailed during the Iran oil shock; dealer takedown in the 2-year was ~24% against a ~10% 12-month average. Jen notes 2-years carry little DV01, so front-end tails matter less than long-end ones. - The 20-year is the wrong canary (short): the 20-year was reintroduced only in 2020 and has little natural demand, a "size 10⅛ shoe," so it structurally trades cheap to 10s and 30s; a 1¼bp tail there is ordinary, not a confidence crisis. - July 2025 7-year: 33% direct, a record, and stopped 2.5bp through after rallying into the auction. Jen "ate her words" from April, when low direct takedown fed fears of a foreign buyer strike. - New bill buyers (stablecoins): the GENIUS Act (July 2025) requires stablecoins to be backed by T-bills and similar assets. Stablecoins outstanding were ~$260B (July 2025), and Bessent projected $2T. More stablecoins mean a structural bid for bills, which pushes front-end yields down without a Fed cut. Kristen calls it a "chip-maker" business model: hold yielding bills, issue a non-yielding token.

Business significance. Auctions are the largest recurring supply events in global finance, so a tail can reprice the whole curve, and with it mortgage rates and corporate issuance windows, within minutes. Corporate treasurers time issuance around auction weeks and refunding months. Weak foreign demand is the single scariest signal for a deficit country, because "there'll always be a buyer of US debt, the question is at what rate" (Adami).

Forces & impact. Supply: deficits and the issuance mix (§9). Demand: foreign reserve managers, banks (balance-sheet capacity), money funds (bills), pensions and insurers (long end), and now stablecoins. Second order: if stablecoins become the marginal bill buyer, the Treasury is pushed to issue shorter, which raises rollover risk. Jen's labeled speculation: weakening the dollar → crypto revival → stablecoin growth → more bill demand, with a Trump family stablecoin business adding a conflict of interest.

With vs. without. Without a predictable calendar the market would have to price issuance-surprise risk into every yield. That predictability is why Jen bristles at influencers calling auction sizes surprising: only the outcomes are news. Without single-price auctions, bidders would shade bids to avoid the winner's curse and raise the government's cost.

Applies when / Breaks when. The bidder-mix signal works only if categories map to real investor types. Auctions function smoothly until dealer balance sheets are full (§9) or a buyer class retreats together (April 2025).

Channel example. The best explanation of Treasury auctions (short); It Wasn't Equity Turmoil That Spooked Trump — It Was the Bond Market (Apr 11 2025); Wall Street is Watching Something More Concerning than Oil (Mar 31 2026); Why the 20 year US Treasury bond auction isn't the canary in the coal mine (short); AI Collusion in Trading, Figma IPO and Could Stablecoins Lower Interest Rates? (late July 2025); If the Fed won't cut, could stablecoins be the key? (short, 2025).

Counterpoint. Likely error: Jen treats direct bidder share as the proxy for foreign governments ("you automatically think China"). The standard reading is the reverse. Foreign official accounts usually bid through the NY Fed and show up as indirect, and directs are largely domestic money managers. Treat her foreign-demand inferences from direct takedown with caution. This matters for the April 2025 story: the April 9 10-year with its tiny direct share also drew a near-record indirect share (~88%) and low dealer takedown, which is the opposite of a foreign buyer strike. The stress that week was in the secondary market, swap spreads and basis unwinds (§10, §11), so "the auctions forced the pause" is a stronger claim than the auction data supports. Stablecoin sizing comes from interested parties (Bessent, Circle's CEO at $10T), and Jen herself flags that as bias.

9 · Treasury buybacks and debt management

What it is. The Treasury can repurchase its own old bonds and fund the purchase with new issuance elsewhere on the curve. It is not QE: no new money is created, and the total debt is unchanged. What changes is where the duration sits and who has to hold it.

How it works. - The "cash for clunkers" problem: old off-the-run bonds such as the 1.375% Aug-2050, issued in 2020 near zero rates, trade near 46 cents after a 400bp+ selloff. Nobody trades them. They clog dealer balance sheets that primary dealers need for mandatory auction bidding. - Program: started in 2024 at ~$2B a month (barely noticed). On Aug 19 2026 Bessent announced it would at least double long-end (10–30y) buybacks, to ~$4B+. The Treasury can reject offers it considers rich, unlike the Fed's price-insensitive QE. - Three ways to fund it, three different effects (Jen): 1. Bills: moves supply to where demand is deepest, almost no duration, a rounding error at bill scale. 2. 2s/5s: adds duration at the front end. Front yields rise and the curve flattens, a stealth hike that does Warsh's tightening while the headline reads "Treasury supports bonds." 3. Treasury General Account cash: injects cash that wasn't in the system. That is effectively QE by the Treasury, and it would undo the logic above. - Jen's "Prestige" thesis (labeled speculation): the market saw yield suppression, while the real trick was option 2, Bessent doing "Warsh's dirty work." Medeiros (Sep 2026) expects options 1 and 2. He doubts option 3 because of the 2027 debt ceiling: draining the TGA in extraordinary measures risks an "accidental default." - Bessent in his own words: his job is to "truncate the very bad outcome", meaning a liquidity failure. Economics is "biology", not physics, and the Treasury slows things down while hedge funds speed them up.

Business significance. The issuance mix is a lever on long yields, and hence on mortgages and corporate long bonds, that doesn't need the Fed. The buyback increase came just before September's heavy IG calendar, including AI hyperscaler issuance. 30-year bonds from Meta were ~40bp wider and Oracle / SpaceX ~60bp wider within a month of issue. Making room in the long end matters for every issuer.

Forces & impact. It shortens the weighted-average maturity of the debt. Bessent had criticized Yellen for not terming out at 1% in 2020. Kristen defends Yellen with hindsight bias (everyone, including her own ARM refinancings, assumed zero rates forever). Jen defends Bessent: terming out now, at 20-year-high yields, could itself trigger a refinancing crisis. The cost is rollover risk: debt that needed no attention for 30 years now needs refinancing in 2–5. "Not kicking the can down the road… kicking the can across the room."

With vs. without. Without buybacks, illiquid off-the-runs sit on dealer balance sheets, shrinking auction capacity, which in a stress event turns into a failed or badly tailed auction. With aggressive buybacks funded short, long yields get a modest anchor, at the price of a structurally shorter debt profile and more frequent refinancing at whatever rates prevail.

Applies when / Breaks when. It is a liquidity tool when used in size. As a yield-control tool it is limited by scale: $4B a month against ~$20B per long-bond auction. It breaks into quasi-QE if funded from the TGA.

Channel example. I got the chance to ask Scott Bessent ONE question (Sep 3 2026, with the 90-second clip as a short); The truth about Bessent's Treasury buybacks (short); Is the Treasury secretly doing QE? (short).

Counterpoint. The "stealth hike" depends on the funding choice, which won't be known until the refunding announcement after the midterms. Druckenmiller (in a WSJ op-ed) argued the move damaged Treasury credibility. The hosts answer with an AI-detection score on his op-ed, which is a jab at the messenger and doesn't address his argument. Buying back bonds at 46 does not "save half the money" in any real sense: the Treasury pays market value and then refinances at today's higher coupons.

10 · Repo, SOFR and interest-rate swaps

What it is. Repo (repurchase agreement) is a short-term loan secured by a bond: you sell Treasuries to a dealer and agree to buy them back tomorrow at a slightly higher price, and that price difference is the overnight general collateral (GC) rate. SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate) is the benchmark computed from those trades. It replaced LIBOR and now sits under most floating-rate loans and swaps. An interest-rate swap exchanges fixed for floating payments on a notional. A receive-fixed swap is a synthetic bond funded at SOFR.

How it works. - Three ways to own 10-year duration (basis-trade episode, Apr 2025), from most to least balance sheet: (1) pay $100mm cash for the bonds; (2) put ~10% down and finance $90mm in repo, pledging the bonds as collateral, "just like buying a house"; (3) go synthetic with futures (§11) or a receive-fixed swap. Real-money investors default to the derivatives because they consume the least balance sheet. - Carry and roll-down on the repo route: a bond with a 5% coupon financed at 4% GC earns 1% a year if nothing moves. That is positive carry. On an upward-sloping curve the bond also rolls down to a lower-yielding maturity as it ages, so its price drifts up even with an unchanged curve. The risk is the floating leg: if overnight repo jumps to 6–10%, the 5% coupon no longer covers the funding. - Synthetic route: receive fixed / pay SOFR on $100mm notional. Same cash flows, no principal, no cash up front (a par swap has zero NPV at inception), but both sides post margin as the NPV moves. After 2008, swaps moved from bilateral contracts to central clearing, because a positive-NPV swap facing Lehman became an unsecured claim in bankruptcy. - LIBOR → SOFR (What is SOFR??, filmed the day after the last USD LIBOR fixing, June 30 2023). LIBOR was a panel of banks self-reporting where they would lend to each other unsecured for terms of 3, 6 or 12 months, so it carried a bank-credit component and could be rigged (and was). SOFR differs in three ways: it is secured by Treasuries (no bank credit risk), it is computed from actual trades rather than submissions, and it is overnight and backward-looking, "basically the same as GC." Fed funds, by contrast, is banks lending reserves to each other unsecured, which is why the two can decouple under stress. - What the switch broke: term SOFR (anything longer than overnight) is a bespoke, bilaterally traded rate available only to some users, with no interdealer market for dealers to hedge in; legacy LIBOR loans needed credit spread adjustments bolted on to compensate lenders for losing the bank- credit component. - Swap spreads = 10y swap rate − 10y on-the-run Treasury yield. Under LIBOR they were positive (swap rates carried bank credit; Treasuries were risk-free): at a 10bp spread and 10s at 5%, you could pay or receive fixed for 10 years at 5.10%. With QE in 2008 they went negative for the first time, 30-year spreads collapsing to roughly −60bp, meaning the market would rather face interbank credit than hold 30-year US credit and its balance-sheet cost. Post-crisis capital rules kept them negative. In April 2025 30-year spreads got close to −100bp. - The sign trap: desk language still treats spreads as if positive, so −20 → −10 is "widening" and −20 → −30 is "tightening." - Swap spreads as a diagnostic (July 2026): if Treasuries were selling off because of idiosyncratic supply (crowding out by tech debt), swap spreads would tighten. They didn't. Jen concludes it wasn't Treasury-specific: "nobody wants anything", meaning insufficient risk premium across asset classes. - Expressing a view in swaps vs. Treasuries (Hornbach, Sep 2025): a curve steepener in the SOFR swap curve would cost "much more" negative carry than the same steepener in Treasuries, so Morgan Stanley recommended the Treasury version (§3).

Business significance. Every corporate floating-rate loan is SOFR + spread, so swaps are how a CFO turns floating into fixed (or the reverse) without refinancing. Pensions and insurers receive fixed in long swaps to match liabilities, which is why Dutch pension reform matters for long-end rates (§3). Swap pricing is also the market's cleanest read on whether a Treasury move is about rates or about Treasury supply and balance sheet. Repo is the hinge of the whole system: Eisman's argument that the dollar's reserve status is safe rests on overnight repo being a multi-trillion-dollar market that runs almost entirely on Treasury collateral (§16).

Forces & impact. Repo rates track Fed policy and reserve scarcity (§7). The Fed keeps the effective rate inside its target range with administered rates: a floor from interest on reserve balances (banks only) and the reverse repo facility (money funds and others lend cash to the Fed), and a ceiling from the standing repo facility and the discount window (the Fed lends cash). Swap spreads track Treasury supply versus dealer balance-sheet capacity and regulation (the supplementary leverage ratio, the central-clearing mandate). When balance sheet is scarce, the synthetic gets relatively more valuable and Treasuries cheapen versus swaps, which is the negative-swap-spread world.

With vs. without. Without swaps, every hedge needs physical bonds and the balance sheet to carry them. Duration management would be costlier and concentrated in the few institutions with balance sheet. Without a deep repo market, Treasuries lose their "cash-equivalent" status, because you can't borrow against them overnight, and their yields must rise to compensate. Without SOFR's transaction base, the benchmark under trillions of loans is whatever a dozen banks say it is.

Applies when / Breaks when. The synthetic-bond equivalence holds while repo funds smoothly. It breaks in funding stress (2019, March 2020), when GC jumps above SOFR expectations, and levered basis and swap-spread positions get hit together. It also breaks when the collateral itself is doubted: Jen reads April 2025's collapse in swap spreads as investors preferring any derivative to owning a cash Treasury.

Channel example. Bond Market Chaos: Unpacking the Basis Trade Blowup Theory (Apr 2025); What is SOFR?? (July 2023); How does an interest rate swap work? (2024); Fixed Income Strategy 101 feat. Matt Hornbach (Sep 2025); Why Jamie Dimon Won't Buy Stocks OR Bonds Right Now (July 2026, swap-spread read).

Counterpoint. The swap-spread inference is sound in direction but swap spreads also move on regulation and dealer capacity, not only on Treasury-specific supply, so "nobody wants Treasuries" and "nobody has balance sheet for Treasuries" look identical on the screen. The 2008 explanation (fear of a QE-driven debt trap) is the hosts' story; the standard account puts more weight on dealer balance-sheet collapse and on swap demand from hedgers. The SOFR video's worries about term-SOFR liquidity date from 2023 and have eased as CME term SOFR became the loan market default.

11 · Treasury futures, cheapest-to-deliver, and the basis trade

What it is. A Treasury futures contract is an exchange-traded promise to deliver Treasuries at a future date (quarterly expiries). It is not tied to one bond: at expiry the short may deliver any bond from a basket of eligible securities, and one of them is mathematically the cheapest to deliver (CTD). The basis is the price gap between that cash bond and the futures contract. The basis trade buys the cheap cash bond, finances it in repo, and sells the rich future, waiting for the two to converge at expiry.

How it works. - Contract mechanics: the 10-year contract (TY) is $100,000 face per contract. You post a small margin to the exchange and are marked daily, so a futures position is inherently levered. A forward is the same promise negotiated bilaterally and unmargined; futures are standardized, cleared and margined (the hosts sort this out on air). - The basket: TY delivers aged notes, not the on-the-run 10-year: recent 7-years, 10-years issued ~3 years ago, even old 30-year bonds with ~7 years left. Jen says the contract really trades like the 7-year point. - Why one bond is "cheapest": deliver the barrels of oil sitting in your backyard, not the ones you have to ship from overseas. For Treasuries the "shipping cost" is the financing, measured as the implied repo rate. To compare bonds with different coupons and maturities, each gets a conversion factor: its price per $1 face if it yielded 6%. A 5¾% bond trades below par at a 6% yield, so its factor is a little under 1 (the video uses 0.99). - Futures DV01 (How to Calculate Treasury Futures DV01): start from the CTD's Macaulay duration, convert to modified duration, then to dollars using price. Take a CTD DV01 of ~6.6 (per 100 face) and the video computes 6.6 × 0.99 = 6.534, so 6.534 / 10,000 × 78,000 contracts × $100,000 = ~$5.1mm per bp. - The trade that prompted it (short, Apr 2025): someone sold 78,000 June TY contracts in thin London hours, the largest Treasury futures block in at least 12 years. At ~$5.1mm per bp, a 5–10bp selloff put the seller up $25–50mm in a day, plus ~$25mm more on the next 5bp. Jen could not tell whether it was an outright short or a hedge against heavy call open interest. - Why futures are structurally rich: real-money buyers (asset managers, pensions, insurers) prefer futures and receive-fixed swaps because they need far less cash and balance sheet than physical bonds (§10). So futures trade rich to the deliverable cash bonds, and the aged bonds in the basket are illiquid ("locked up in the hands of a little retiree here and a pension fund there"). - The basis trade: a hedge fund buys the cheap cash bonds, finances them in repo, and sells futures against them. Convergence at expiry is near-certain, but the gap is "only a couple of basis points," so it must be levered ~20:1 on average and, per the Money Stuff podcast the hosts cite, up to 100:1. Apollo's chief economist Torsten Sløk estimated the trade at ~$800B (from hedge-fund futures shorts and prime-brokerage repo). - How it breaks: the trade needs two things to stay true, futures rich to cash, and the ability to hold until convergence. A shock that makes cash Treasuries cheapen sharply against futures (a tariff announcement, a repo spike) produces mark-to-market losses multiplied by the leverage, margin calls on the futures leg, and forced selling of the illiquid cash leg, which cheapens it further. March 2020 was the last full blowup; September 2019's repo spike was the funding version (§7).

Business significance. The basis trade is how a cash-futures arbitrage becomes a source of Treasury market liquidity: basis funds absorb the cash bonds that real money doesn't want to hold and supply the futures real money does want. That keeps Treasury yields lower than they would otherwise be, which matters to every borrower priced off them. The cost is a concentrated, levered, short-volatility position sitting in the plumbing of the risk-free asset. For a corporate treasurer, futures DV01 is also the practical hedge unit: pre-hedging a bond issue means shorting the number of contracts whose DV01 matches the planned issue.

Forces & impact. Size grows with the structural richness of futures, which grows with balance-sheet regulation (SLR, Basel endgame) and with real money's preference for derivatives. Risk rises with leverage, repo volatility and reserve scarcity. Jen's April 2025 list of what the Fed could do to relieve the pressure, in order of impact: loosen SLR so banks can hold Treasuries more cheaply; reverse QT into QE; bid directly at auctions; and only last, cut rates ("filing my nails" to lose ten pounds). Her central call is that the basis unwind was a symptom, not the cause: the reported blowups (one PM out $140mm, another $30mm, an unconfirmed $400mm) were large for people and tiny against a $36T market, while the simultaneous collapse in swap spreads pointed to a broad aversion to cash Treasuries.

With vs. without. Without basis traders, futures would trade persistently rich, cash Treasuries cheap, and the cost of the deficit would be higher. With them, the market works well until a shock forces them all to sell the same illiquid bonds at once, which is why the Fed ended up buying Treasuries in size in March 2020. The policy argument that followed (central clearing, SLR reform, a standing repo facility) is an argument about whether to keep the liquidity and socialize the tail.

Applies when / Breaks when. Convergence holds at expiry by construction. The trade breaks when the path to expiry is intolerable: repo spikes, margin increases, or a sudden repricing of Treasuries as an asset class rather than of one bond.

Channel example. Bond Market Chaos: Unpacking the Basis Trade Blowup Theory. Cause… or Convenient Excuse? (Apr 2025); Largest 10 Year Treasury Futures Block Trade EVER? (short, Apr 2025); How to Calculate Treasury Futures DV01 (Calculating & Converting DV01 of the Cheapest to Deliver); Head of US Macro… (Jan 2026: the trade back to sizes "not seen since… 2019").

Counterpoint. Formula error in the DV01 video: the futures contract tracks the CTD divided by its conversion factor, so futures DV01 ≈ CTD DV01 ÷ CF, not ×. With CF 0.99 the answer is 6.6 / 0.99 ≈ 6.67, or ~$5.2mm per bp: barely different here, very different for low-coupon CTDs with factors far below 1. The video's "6½ to just under 8 years" basket is the practical CTD zone; the CME specification for TY runs from 6½ to 10 years remaining. Jen is careful to say she cannot see the flows and knew the PMs involved, which is honest, but "symptom not cause" is also the view most comfortable for someone who thinks the real story is a repricing of US policy. The Money Stuff "100:1" is an upper-tail anecdote, not a market average.

12 · Mortgage-rate drivers and housing policy

What it is. A US 30-year fixed mortgage is a risk-free rate plus a spread, and the risk-free rate is the 10-year Treasury, not the 30-year. Borrowers move or refinance, so the mortgage's effective life and rate sensitivity are much shorter than its stated term.

How it works. - Banks originate mortgages, securitize them (with a Fannie/Freddie guarantee taking out most credit risk), and sell the MBS so they can lend again. - MBS investors bear rate risk, (guaranteed-away) credit risk, and prepayment risk. US borrowers can prepay without penalty, which makes the holder short an option, so MBS have negative convexity. - Partial durations: decompose MBS price sensitivity by curve point (2y, 5y, 10y, 30y), measured empirically. Hornbach's figures (Sep 2025): only ~10% of a secondary-market 30-year mortgage's rate sensitivity sits on the 30-year Treasury, ~40% on the 10-year, and the remaining ~50% on the 2- and 5-year. So mortgages trade roughly as 10y + spread, with real front-end exposure, and pushing only the 30-year down 100bp would barely move housing. If Bessent wants cheaper mortgages, he wants all yields lower, not a flatter curve. - Why Fed cuts transmit less than they used to (Patton, Sep 2024): of an ~$8T agency mortgage market, ~35% was adjustable before the GFC (her figure, likely the origination peak), so policy moves hit household payments directly; today under 1% floats. TCW estimated 85% of mortgages in the Bloomberg Agg would not be economic to refinance until rates fell another ~100bp. That is lock-in measured. - The predatory mechanics of 2006 (Steve Eisman): subprime loans carried a 2–3 year teaser (say 3%) resetting to LIBOR + 600 (~9%), underwritten to the teaser the borrower could afford, with ~4 points of origination fees rolled into principal against ~1 point on a prime loan. At reset the lender offered a refinance into the same structure for another 4 points, so the borrower never escaped and the originator earned fees on a loop. Subprime origination went from ~$50B (2002) to ~$500B (2006), 2% to 20% of the market. Rising delinquencies in 2006-vintage securitizations were his signal. - Iran war, March 2026: the Fed held, yet 30y mortgages rose from 5.75% (end Feb) to 6.5%, because oil-driven inflation fear lifted the long end. The Fed sets overnight rates. The market sets the long end. - GSE purchases: Trump directed Fannie/Freddie to buy $200B of MBS. The agency market is $9T+, and one estimate cited puts the effect at ~15bp of spread. The purchases also push the GSEs toward post-2008 retained-portfolio caps. Jen reads it as a midterm signal more than a rate fix. - 50-year mortgage: roughly 15% lower annual payment than a 30-year at the then-current curve. In an amortizing loan, early payments are almost all interest, so equity barely builds ("almost like you're renting"). The portable variant breaks the collateral logic of lending (a $1mm loan moving to a $500k house) and makes the borrower's option close to certain to be worth exercising, so lenders would charge a much higher rate.

Business significance. Housing is the largest household asset and a main transmission channel. The 2020 lock-in (2% mortgages nobody will give up) freezes turnover, labor mobility, and the revenue of brokers, builders and movers. For the Fed, falling mortgage rates now risk re-igniting house prices and rents, which had been the main source of disinflation. That is why Medeiros says Treasury and Fed want opposite things for mortgage rates in 2026.

Forces & impact. Long-end term premium (the dominant 2025–26 driver, more than spreads), MBS spreads, GSE policy, and lock-in. Every proposal on the table (GSE buying, the 50-year, portability, banning institutional single-family purchases) is demand-side. With supply fixed, more buying power means higher prices. Housing starts and permits per capita sit near 50-year lows. Institutional investors took ~18% of single-family purchases (flow, Redfin, ~12 months) but hold only ~1% of the stock.

With vs. without. Without GSE guarantees and free prepayment, the US would look like most countries: shorter fixes, more floating-rate risk on households, and a smaller, more volatile housing market. Without the 2008 and 2020 QE, the hosts argue, prices would not be where they are. Medeiros: the proposals make him more bullish on house prices troughing in 12–18 months, and no better on affordability.

Applies when / Breaks when. "10y + spread" holds in normal prepayment regimes. It breaks when the lock-in collapses prepayment speeds (MBS extend toward longer duration), or when spreads, not Treasuries, drive the move (2008).

The original version of this note put the partial-duration hotspot at 7–10y from a short; Hornbach's breakdown gives the front end more weight than that, and the two are model-dependent estimates that shift with prepayment speeds. 13 · Inflation measurement and pass-through

What it is. Inflation is the rate of change in prices, not their level: "the height of each stair." The US has two baskets. CPI (BLS) is household-survey based with fixed annual weights. PCE (BEA) is business-receipts based, its weights shift continuously, and it includes spending made on consumers' behalf (e.g. employer health care). The Fed targets PCE, watches core (ex food and energy) and "supercore" (core services ex housing), and uses CPI for direction.

How it works. - Substitution: beef triples in price. CPI still assumes you eat burgers, while PCE registers the switch to chicken (or, on Burton's evidence, a husband who has bought pork at Wegmans every week). - Receipts vs. survey: ask three patients what an MRI costs and you hear $300, $1,500 or $0. The hospital records $1,500 each time. - Base effects: readings are year-over-year, so a soft print last March makes this March look hot. Burton expected a mid-to-high-3s March 2026 CPI partly for that reason. Prices can stay elevated while measured inflation reads zero. - Tariff pass-through: inventory days = inventory / COGS × days. Nike: $7.5B / $6.6B × 90 = ~102 days of cushion before tariffs hit shelf prices. Munchkin (made in China, 145% tariff): $100k of goods now costs $245k landed, with the US importer paying the tariff. Medeiros estimates ~60% pass-through, a stated rate of ~18% but an effective rate nearer ~10% after exemptions. - Oil: jet fuel → airfares is the second-round effect the Fed fears when household expectations are already elevated. The oil CEO's rule of thumb is transcribed as "every 10 cents ≈ 0.2% of global inflation", almost certainly $10/bbl, not 10 cents. - Nominal vs. real, and what a breakeven is: John Normand's definition (2024): the nominal rate is what you observe; the real rate is nominal minus inflation, your gain in purchasing power. In 2024 the US had positive real rates and Japan negative ones, the widest gap in ~30 years (§15). The market's version uses TIPS: a 10-year nominal Treasury yield minus the 10-year TIPS real yield is the breakeven, the inflation rate at which the two pay the same. (The channel's dedicated breakeven video is not in the transcript set, so this decomposition is supplied here, not taught on air.) The hosts' July 2026 reference to real yields "low-to-mid 2%" is a reading of this market. Hornbach, who made markets in cash TIPS in 2005–06, calls it the worst market-making job on the Street: a handful of dealers, thin liquidity, and drawdowns management has to stomach. - One-time level shift vs. ongoing inflation (Hornbach, Kristen, Sep 2025): a tariff, like Japan's consumption-tax rises, should lift the price level once and then drop out of the year-over-year rate (base effects again), while cutting real demand. What keeps it inflationary is uncertainty: nobody knows the split between exporter, importer and consumer, or whether the rate will change next month.

Business significance. The Fed's reaction function runs on these numbers, so every pricing, wage and debt decision indirectly reads PCE. For operators, inventory days are the lead indicator for when a cost shock reaches the P&L. They also give you a window to reprice, re-source or pre-buy.

Forces & impact. Supply shocks (oil, tariffs), demand (fiscal impulse), expectations, and base effects. Second order: exogenous shocks the Fed can't control show up in headline inflation, and the policy question is whether they bleed into core. Since 2019 inflation has been higher everywhere (Levine), as every government spent and cut rates at once in 2020–21.

With vs. without. Without PCE's substitution adjustment, measured inflation overstates the cost of living and the Fed over-tightens. Without core measures, the Fed would react to every oil spike it can't control. The cost is that core can look benign while households feel the headline. That is Kristen's Main Street point: flights she bought for $350 now cost ~$1,000.

Applies when / Breaks when. Core is a good guide when shocks are transitory. It fails when shocks persist long enough to reset expectations ("half a decade of transitory," Medeiros).

Channel example.
