14 · FX and the dollar

What it is. An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. It is driven by growth, inflation, central-bank policy, fiscal policy, political stability, and above all rate differentials. Raising rates should strengthen a currency.

How it works. - Rate differential: the dollar strengthened through the 2022–23 Fed hiking cycle. The yen kept weakening even as the BOJ hiked, because the gap stayed wide (Adami). - Reserve recycling: decades of US trade deficits shipped dollars abroad, and those dollars were recycled into Treasuries. Tariffs that shrink those flows also shrink foreign demand for US debt (Jen, Apr 2025). - Defending a currency without dumping Treasuries: Japan, the largest foreign holder, can pledge Treasuries in the Fed's foreign repo facility for cash instead of selling them. Jen notes Bessent had pushed to expand it. In summer 2026 the US and Japan ran the largest coordinated intervention in decades; Bessent's "to-do list: buy 5–10 billion yen" became a meme. - Why a weak dollar tempts: US debt is fixed in nominal dollars, so a weaker dollar transfers value away from foreign holders. Officially "we want a strong dollar" (Bessent); unofficially, Jen notes, Trump says the quiet part out loud. - De-dollarization: after the 2022 sanctions on Russia's central bank, non-aligned central banks bought gold instead of Treasuries (Levine). That flow accelerated after April 2 2025. The dollar fell ~10% in H1 2025. - Pegs, crawling pegs and the RMB (FX101 episode and short, Apr 2025): China's renminbi (units: yuan) is not free-floating. From the mid-1990s it was pegged to the dollar at an artificially low rate, maintained by buying dollars, which built China into an export power. In 2005 it moved to an undisclosed basket within a tight band (a "dirty float" or crawling peg), effectively re-pegged in 2008, and devalued in 2015 and 2019, each feeding US "currency manipulator" charges. When an influencer cited the yuan at an 18-year low as proof the US was "winning" the trade war, Jen's answer was that the dollar was falling too: "we are losing together." - Who wins from a weak dollar: a weaker currency helps a country that depends on exports and hurts its consumers abroad (Kristen's vacation framing). For a consumption-heavy importer like the US it is a strange goal, which is why the hosts read dollar weakness in April 2025 as a warning rather than a win. - Hedging costs drive flows (Hornbach, Sep 2025): a Japanese investor who buys US stocks and sells the dollars forward to strip out FX risk pays roughly the rate differential to do so. As the Fed cuts, that hedge gets cheaper, foreigners hedge more, and hedging means selling dollars forward. Morgan Stanley called the dollar down from early 2025 (against consensus) and saw ~10% more to go. - Trade construction (FX desk short): "short cable" means short GBP/USD at ~1.30, target 1.25, stop 1.35. The trainee is mocked for a symmetric, coin-flip risk/reward with no thesis. Jen's lesson: the manager should have coached the inputs and logic rather than hazing her.

Business significance. For importers the dollar sets landed cost. For exporters it sets competitiveness. For the Treasury it sets foreign appetite for its auctions. Medeiros calls the dollar the relief valve: if markets start to believe policy will be set well below where it should be, the dollar falls first, and then inflation expectations follow.

Forces & impact. Policy credibility (§6), rate gaps, capital repatriation (US equities lagged the rest of the developed world over 12 months to Jan 2026 even with AI), and sanctions risk. Second order: a weaker dollar helps gold, crypto and (on Jen's speculation) stablecoins, which feeds back into bill demand (§8).

With vs. without. Without the dollar's reserve role, the US would borrow at a higher term premium and could not run persistent deficits as cheaply. The hosts treat losing it as the tail risk behind April 2025: "for the first time in my lifetime." Without intervention capacity, Japan's only defense would be selling Treasuries, which would push US yields up (Adami).

Applies when / Breaks when. The rate-differential rule holds in normal regimes. It breaks when credibility or fiscal fear dominates. In 2025 the dollar fell even as US rates stayed high.

Channel example. I got the chance to ask Scott Bessent (Sep 2026, intervention and de-dollarization); What You Must Know About Commodities feat. Guy Adami (2024, yen); Time to Sell? feat. Matt Hornbach (Sep 2025).

Counterpoint. "A weak dollar means we owe foreigners less" is true of their purchasing power. It also raises US import prices and future borrowing costs, so it is not a free deleveraging. Lloyd Blankfein's retort, relayed by Kristen, is the strongest counter to de-dollarization panic: where else would they put the money? Jen's RMB history is self-described cliff notes ("not an FX expert"); the broad sequence is right, though the 1994 unification and the 2005–08 managed appreciation (~20%) are compressed. Hornbach's 2020 short-dollar call took months to work, which he concedes.

15 · Carry and the yen carry trade

What it is. Carry is what a position earns (or costs) if nothing moves: the difference between the rate you receive on what you own and the rate you pay to fund it. Jen's correction of the private-equity usage: carry here is the gap between where you invest and where you fund, not carried interest. A carry trade borrows in a low-yielding currency and invests in a high-yielding one. The yen carry trade is the canonical version: borrow yen near zero, buy dollars (or Aussie dollars, or emerging-market currencies) and pocket the differential.

How it works. - Exchange rate as the price of two monies (John Normand, ex-JPM head of cross-asset strategy, now at AustralianSuper; spring 2024): one money pays X, the other pays Y, and a lot of cash simply moves from low yield to high yield. In 2024 US real rates were positive and Japan's negative, a gap near a 30-year wide, and dollar/yen sat near a 30-year high. That is the carry trade showing up in the spot rate. - Why the yen: after the Nikkei bubble burst in 1989–90, deflation pinned Japanese rates near zero for three decades, so the yen became the safe funding currency. - The payoff shape: "up by the stairs, down by the elevator shaft." Long stretches of low-volatility gains in the high-yielder, then a macro shock in the high-yield economy (commodities halving in the GFC crushed the Brazilian real, Mexican peso, Aussie and Kiwi) wipes out years of carry in weeks. The skill is timing the shock, and most people don't. - Normand's 2024 forecast: Fed cuts ~75bp over the cycle, the BOJ hikes ~100bp once a quarter, the differential narrows but still favors the dollar, global demand for US AI equities keeps the dollar bid, and the yen appreciates 5–10% at most. - Carry elsewhere in this note: a bond financed in repo (5% coupon − 4% GC = +1%, plus roll-down, §10); a curve steepener as negative carry, paid as rent while you wait (§3); Eisman's 2006 subprime short, where shorting New Century stock cost ~20% a year in dividends plus borrow while buying protection on the BBB− tranche two floors up the "building" cost ~3%. Same view, one-seventh the carry. - 2026 coda (Feb 2026 episode): the BOJ hiking, Japanese underlying inflation near target and a weak yen while the Nikkei set records. For Japan, after decades fighting deflation, higher rates read as good news, and the summer 2026 joint US–Japan intervention (§14) was the policy response to the yen end of the trade.

Business significance. Carry trades move trillions across borders, so they set exchange rates for every importer, exporter and foreign investor. An equity investor who ignores the currency can see a good stock trade turned into a bad one by a 20% FX gap in a quarter (Normand). For a corporate treasurer, borrowing in the low-rate currency is the same trade: cheap until the funding currency jumps.

Forces & impact. Rate differentials (central-bank paths in both countries), volatility (carry works when vol is low and dies when it spikes), risk appetite, and capital flows into the high-yielder's assets. Second order: because everyone is short the same funding currency, an unwind forces simultaneous buying of it, so the funding currency rallies into a crisis, and the move feeds on itself.

With vs. without. Without carry trades, interest-rate gaps would sit unarbitraged and currencies would track trade flows more closely; high-rate economies would attract less foreign capital. With them, capital flows to yield in calm times and stampedes back in shocks, which exports one country's easy money into another's asset prices.

Applies when / Breaks when. Works when the differential is wide and stable and volatility is low. Breaks on a shock to the high-yielder, on a surprise from the funding central bank, or when positioning gets crowded enough that a small move forces stop-outs.

Channel example. Finance, Philosophy, and the Yen Carry Trade feat. John Normand (2024); Tariffs 101 (Apr 2025, carry as the reason a dovish Fed should weaken the dollar); Steve Eisman, the Real-Life "Big Short" Investor (Apr 2025, negative carry of the New Century short); SaaS-pocalypse, misleading jobs data, and Japanese equities breaking records (Feb 2026).

Counterpoint. Normand's "5–10% max" was overrun within months: in July–September 2024 dollar/yen fell from ~161 to ~140, roughly 13%, in a violent carry unwind after a BOJ hike and weak US data, which is the elevator shaft he described arriving faster than he forecast. Kristen's phrase "intervention from the Bank of Japan" is loose: Japan's Ministry of Finance decides FX intervention and the BOJ executes it. Normand works for a pension fund and is selling a long-horizon, stay-invested view; carry is one input to currencies, not the whole model, as he says himself.

16 · Tariffs and the April 2025 safe-haven break

What it is. A tariff is a tax on imports, paid by the importing business to its own government. Who ultimately bears it depends on who gives up margin. The April 2025 "reciprocal" tariffs turned that textbook question into a market event: for the first time in the hosts' careers, US stocks, Treasuries and the dollar sold off together, which is not what a safe haven does.

How it works. - Incidence, in three branches (Tariffs 101 and short): a foreign maker sells a microphone to a US importer for $50; the importer marks it up $50; the consumer pays $100. Add a $10 tariff, paid to US Customs, and either the foreign maker cuts to $40, or the US importer cuts its markup to $40, or the consumer pays $110 (or buys something else). Most near-term cost was expected to land on US firms and consumers, because exporters weren't willing parties and many US firms run thin margins. - The reciprocal formula (Apr 2 2025): take US goods imports from a country minus US exports to it, divide by imports, call that the country's "tariff rate," then halve it. Imports $200, exports $100: (200 − 100) / 200 = 50%, halved to 25%. Floor of 10% on everyone. Results: China 34% on top of an existing 20%, EU 20%, Japan 24%, autos 25%, Canada and Mexico already at 25% (Canadian energy 10%), and an uninhabited penguin island on the list. The formula measures the goods trade deficit, not any tariff the other country charges, and ignores services, where the US runs a surplus. - History the hosts used: the Fordney–McCumber Act (1922) took average import duties to ~40%; Smoot–Hawley (1930) added ~20% more on everything, drew retaliation and deepened the Depression; the Reciprocal Tariff Act (1934), postwar GATT and the WTO then ran a century of liberalization. Trump's first term (2018: washing machines and solar at 30–50%, steel and aluminum 10–25%) was largely kept by Biden. - The macro read: tariffs mean slower growth and higher prices, i.e. stagflation. Markets priced the Fed fighting the growth side (more cuts), and Jen predicted a steeper curve: companies would "lever their way out" rather than grow out. - The break (Apr 2–11 2025): equities fell, the 10-year rallied briefly to ~3.9% and then sold off to ~4.5%, the dollar hit a 3-year low and gold soared. With a risk-off move, safe-haven demand should have strengthened the dollar and pulled yields down. It did neither. The hosts read it as the market pricing a real chance that the dollar loses reserve status, plus the auction evidence in §8; the 90-day pause came minutes after the 10-year auction. - The plumbing link: the world earns dollars by selling to the US and recycles them into dollar assets, mainly Treasuries (foreigners hold ~25–30%). Fewer imports mean fewer recycled dollars, so trade policy is also Treasury-demand policy (§14). - The "deliberate crash to refinance" theory (short and Apr 11 episode): ~$9.1T of debt rolls each year out of $36.2T, so lower rates would help. But the Fed sets only the front end, the rolling debt is mostly bills, and long yields rose. The hosts treat the theory as debunked by the price action. - GDP fallout (Apr 30 2025 episode): Q1 GDP contracted (advance −0.3%) as firms pulled imports forward ahead of tariffs, with net exports subtracting ~5 points. Jen expected the same next quarter. - The fiscal contradiction: if tariffs are a negotiating tactic ending in a few 5–20% deals, they raise too little to dent the deficit; if they are meant to fund tax cuts, they must be high and permanent. The equity market was pricing both at once.

Business significance. For operators, the questions are incidence and lead time: who in your supply chain eats the tax, and how many days of inventory you have before it reaches shelf prices (§13). Small importers are hit hardest because large firms can lobby for carve-outs. For capital markets, the episode is the clearest live demonstration that the US "risk-free" rate has a credibility component.

Forces & impact. Trade balances, retaliation, inventory cycles, the reserve-currency recycling loop, and political feedback (the administration reversed course when bond and equity markets moved together). Second order: higher input costs tighten leverage covenants and widen credit spreads (§1), private equity exits stall, and LPs over-allocated to illiquid assets seek secondaries.

With vs. without. Without tariffs since the 1930s, the US built the world's deepest consumer market and the dollar's reserve role on trade deficits recycled into Treasuries. With sweeping tariffs imposed at once, that recycling loop is put at risk, and the hosts' fear is a vacuum filled by a basket of allied currencies or gold.

Applies when / Breaks when. Incidence logic always applies; the split depends on pricing power and substitutes. The safe-haven assumption applies while the US is seen as the safest counterparty; it broke, briefly, when US policy itself became the shock.

Channel example. Tariffs 101: Why the Markets and U.S. Dollar Are Tanking (Apr 4 2025); What are tariffs and how do they work? and Is Trump deliberately trying to crash the U.S. stock markets? (shorts); It Wasn't Equity Turmoil That Spooked Trump — It Was the Bond Market (Apr 11 2025); Steve Eisman, the Real-Life "Big Short" Investor, on Tariff Panic (Apr 11 2025); From Intern to Offer… (Plus Some Markets and Tariff Talk) (Apr 30 2025).

Counterpoint. Steve Eisman, recorded the same afternoon, is the strongest counter and the hosts air him in full. His case: the tariffs answer a real grievance (NAFTA and China's WTO entry grew GDP but hollowed out towns), and the US holds the cards because exports are only ~11% of US GDP versus ~19% officially for China (he guesses ~30% counting transshipment), 30%+ for Europe, 40%+ for Germany and ~35% for Canada and Mexico, 25 points of it to the US. Partners will negotiate. On the dollar: the global financial system runs on Treasuries, overnight repo is trillions of dollars collateralized by them, and "there is no alternative." He told Jen she sounded hysterical, and she owned it ("I'm a bond girl"). The market partly agreed with him: equities recovered to near pre-April levels within weeks. Other corrections: the GDP discussion leaves investment out of the GDP identity (inventories absorbed much of the import surge), and Jen's "another hit next quarter" was wrong, as Q2 printed about +3% when imports collapsed. The 1970s "rates north of 20%" was 1980–81 under Volcker. And the hosts' insistence that they are apolitical sits awkwardly with episodes that are, by their own account, mostly opinion on a policy.

17 · Recession indicators

What it is. These are signals that the cycle is turning. The serious ones are the inverted yield curve, labor-market breakevens, and credit and financial conditions. The folklore ones are consumer-behavior proxies that sometimes rhyme with spending stress.

How it works. - Curve: every inversion has preceded a recession by 18–36 months. Adami's refinement is that the re-steepening after a long inversion is the danger signal, not the inversion itself. The 2022–24 inversion was the longest on record, and there was no recession. - Labor breakeven: 90% of labor-force growth since Q3 2023 was foreign-born. With immigration reversing, the payroll gain needed to hold unemployment steady falls to ~40–50k/month (Medeiros, Jan 2026). 75k a month is then tightening, not weakness. Payroll headlines must be read against a moving breakeven. - First prints vs. revisions (Feb 2026): January payrolls printed +130k against ~70k expected and the market priced out a March cut. Jen's point was the revisions: 2025's monthly average gain was cut from ~49k to ~15k, with Challenger layoffs at post-GFC highs. Discount first prints when the pattern is revision after negative revision. - How a macro PM trades the print (Ashish Goyal, ex-BlueCrest/Citadel/Balyasny, early 2024): a 250k payroll against 200k expected moves front-end yields 5–15bp, about one cut priced out. If the broader trend still points to cuts, keep receiving into the move. The hard part is surviving the path: stop-losses on a $100mm book shrank from ~$10–12mm fifteen years ago to ~$4–6mm. - GDP is backward-looking (Apr 2025): Q1 2025's contraction was mostly tariff front-running in imports, and reversed the next quarter. Confidence surveys and inflation expectations are the forward-looking exceptions. - Folklore (two shorts): the hemline index (1926), lipstick (Lauder, 2001), high heels, cardboard-box demand ("very real", reportedly watched by the Fed), men's underwear (attributed to Greenspan), plus the hosts' own joke "Bravo index" (Real Housewives 2008; Scandoval and SVB 2023). - Allocator rule (Levine): the question is not "will stocks fall?" but "is there a recession?" At ≤30% recession probability, stay invested. In 2025 the S&P returned 16.5% fully invested and roughly −12% if you missed the 10 best days, all of which followed the worst days in April. Buying at all-time highs has historically not lowered 1/3/5-year returns (BNY study).

Business significance. Recession probability sets hiring plans, inventory, capex timing and debt tenor. Getting the breakeven wrong means misreading a healthy labor market as weak (or the reverse) and cutting too early.

Forces & impact. Curve signals work through bank margins and credit supply with long lags. In 2023–25 the lag was broken by fiscal support and a private sector that had locked in low rates, which made the economy less rate-sensitive (§3). AI could change the growth–employment relationship ("a coefficient shift"), which would make historical breakevens unreliable.

With vs. without. Without leading indicators, firms react to recessions after the layoffs. With overfit indicators, they de-risk into a boom, which is the 2023 "recession that never happened" (Levine: "we're still waiting for the recession of 2020").

Applies when / Breaks when. The curve works when the inversion reflects restrictive policy. It weakens when the long end is suppressed by QE or flight-to-quality, or when term premium is structurally changing. The folklore indices are entertainment. The hosts present them that way, and only cardboard-box demand has a plausible economic mechanism.

Channel example. Top 5 wildest recession indicators / Top 10… signs (shorts); Every New Fed Chair… (curve inversion 2006); Commodities feat. Guy Adami (2024); Time to Sell? feat. Alicia Levine (Jan 2026); SaaS-pocalypse, misleading jobs data… (Feb 2026); Portfolio Manager at World's Top Hedge Funds… Breaks Down Global Macro Trading (2024); From Intern to Offer… (Apr 2025).

Counterpoint. Levine runs a wealth-management business whose clients stay invested, so "stay invested" is good advice and good for her business. The 10-best-days stat ignores that you also miss the worst days, and that the two cluster together. "Every inversion preceded a recession" survives only if 2022–24 is still "early." Jen's "January is a head fake" was a labeled view, and the revision arithmetic as transcribed (~43k total) doesn't match a 49k → 15k monthly cut, which implies ~400k over a year; check the BLS benchmark before reusing it.

How the concepts connect

Tariffs (§16) / oil shock ──► headline inflation (§13) ──► Fed reaction function (§4, §5)
     │        │                                                   │
     │        │                          front end reprices ◄─────┘  (futures odds, DV01 losses §2)
     │        ▼
     │  inflation expectations ──► long-end term premium (§3) ◄── deficits, long-end supply,
     │        │                         ▲                         hyperscaler issuance, pension unwind
     │        │        credibility / independence (§6) ──► the dollar = relief valve (§14)
     │        │                                                   │
     │        │                    rate gaps ──► carry trades (§15) ──► elevator-shaft unwinds
     ▼        ▼
fewer recycled dollars ──► weaker auction demand (§8) ──► 10-year yield
                                                              │
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     ▼                                                        ▼
mortgage = 10y + spread (§12)                corporate yield = 10y + credit spread (§1)
     │                                                        │
housing politics ──► GSE buying               covenant math ──► spreads widen
                                                              │
Treasury response: buybacks + issuance mix (§9) ──► shorter WAM ──► rollover risk
     │                                     │
bill supply ◄── stablecoins, Fed bill      repo / reserves plumbing (§7, §10)
     reinvestment (§7, §8)                       │
                                                 ▼
             cash vs futures vs swaps (§10, §11): balance sheet decides who holds duration
                                                 │
                     levered basis trade (§11) ──► forced selling when repo or cash cheapens
                                                    (2019, Mar 2020, Apr 2025 template)

April 2025 ran across the top of this chart: tariffs threatened the dollar-recycling loop, so Treasuries, the dollar and stocks fell together; swap spreads collapsed and basis trades unwound as cash Treasuries cheapened against derivatives; and the administration paused within a week. The 2026 sequence ran down the middle. The Iran oil spike lifted 2s and 10s 50–60bp (macro funds lost on DV01 and crowded steepeners). Mortgages rose 75bp with the Fed on hold. Political pressure to "do something" about affordability produced GSE buying and Treasury buybacks. The Treasury's issuance choice may have tightened the front end even as it supported the back. And a balance-sheet-hawk chair hiked because financial conditions, not the policy rate, were the true measure of tightness. Underneath both, the question of who has balance sheet to hold duration (real money in futures and swaps, levered funds in cash bonds, dealers forced to take down auctions) decides how violently a shock moves yields. The single recurring lesson: the Fed controls one point on the curve. Everything a business actually borrows at is set by the market, and in 2025–26 by the Treasury, the GSEs and the plumbing as well.

Retrieval questions

  1. The Fed holds rates steady but mortgage rates jump 75bp. How? Mortgages price off the 10-year plus a spread. An oil shock lifted inflation expectations and term premium at the long end, which the Fed doesn't set.
  2. Two traders each lose on a $100mm Treasury position. The 2-year moved 60bp, the 10-year 50bp. Who lost more, and why do desks avoid this comparison? The 10-year trader: duration 8 vs. 1.8, so ~$4mm vs. ~$1.1mm. Desks size by DV01, not notional, so risk is comparable across maturities.
  3. Treasury yields fall in a tariff panic. Why might a leveraged company's borrowing cost still rise? Its yield = risk-free + credit spread. Lower EBITDA pushes leverage toward covenant limits (4× → 8× on unchanged debt), and spreads widen more than Treasuries fall.
  4. Fed funds futures for a 30-day month price at 96.29, the effective rate is 3.63, and the meeting is on day 16. What hike probability is priced? (30×3.71 − 16×3.63)/14 = 3.80; (3.80−3.63)/0.25 ≈ 68%.
  5. Why is a Fed buying $71B of Treasuries at auction during QT not QE? It is reinvesting most of $76B of maturing SOMA holdings. The balance sheet still shrinks, and no net new reserves are created to push long yields down.
  6. The Treasury doubles long-end buybacks. Under which funding choice is this a stealth tightening, and under which is it QE-like? Funded with 2s/5s it adds front-end duration supply, which raises front yields and flattens the curve. Funded from TGA cash it injects new liquidity, which looks like QE.
  7. Why can a dovish appointee not simply cut rates? The FOMC is a 12-vote majority committee, and the chair has no veto. Miran could only dissent.
  8. Medeiros says policy is loose with the 10-year at 4.15%. What is his evidence, and its weakness? 10y yields ~300bp below nominal GDP growth, easing financial conditions, IG demand at the tights. The weakness: one quarter's 8% NGDP flatters it, and trend nominal growth is lower.
  9. Why would a portable 50-year mortgage carry a much higher rate than a 30-year? The collateral can change, and the borrower's option to keep a low rate becomes near-certain to be valuable, so the lender is short a much more expensive option. The DV01 difference between 30 and 50 years is small.
  10. The curve bull-steepens in the US and bear-steepens in Europe in the same year. What different stories do they tell? US: front-end yields fell on expected cuts. Europe: long-end yields rose on fiscal-driven term premium despite ~200bp of ECB cuts. The policy rate and the long end decoupled.
  11. Why does the Fed prefer PCE to CPI? It captures substitution in real time and spending made on consumers' behalf, so it describes total consumer spending, the behavior rate policy targets.

  12. A record share of direct bidders at a 7-year auction. What can and can't you infer? Strong demand (it stopped 2.5bp through). Foreign official demand mostly shows up as indirect bids via the NY Fed, so reading "direct = China" is unreliable.

  13. A real-money manager can get 10-year exposure by paying cash, financing in repo, buying futures or receiving fixed in a swap. Why does that choice make futures trade rich to cash bonds? Futures and swaps use far less balance sheet, so real money crowds into them; the deliverable cash bonds are left cheap, which is the gap basis traders lever up to capture.

  14. Why can a near-riskless convergence trade blow up a hedge fund? The gap is a few bp, so it needs 20:1 or more leverage; a shock that cheapens cash against futures, or a repo spike, produces mark-to-market losses and margin calls before expiry, forcing sales of illiquid bonds into a falling market.
  15. You are short 78,000 TY contracts; the CTD has DV01 6.6 and conversion factor 0.99. What is your risk per bp, and what is wrong with the video's method? ≈ 6.6 / 0.99 / 10,000 × 78,000 × $100,000 ≈ $5.2mm. The video multiplies by the factor (≈ $5.1mm); futures track the CTD price divided by its factor.
  16. Swap spreads go from −20bp to −30bp. Is that widening or tightening, and what might it say? Tightening, by desk convention inherited from the positive-spread LIBOR era. Treasuries are cheapening against swaps: scarce dealer balance sheet, heavy supply, or aversion to holding cash Treasuries (April 2025).
  17. Why did SOFR replace LIBOR, and what did the switch remove from the benchmark? LIBOR was self-reported, unsecured and manipulable; SOFR is computed from secured overnight Treasury repo trades. The switch removed the bank-credit and term components, which is why legacy loans needed credit spread adjustments and term SOFR is thin.
  18. A carry trade has earned steady returns for three years. What does its history say about the next month? Little, except that losses arrive suddenly: carry pays "up by the stairs" and unwinds "down the elevator shaft" when the high-yielder suffers a shock or the funding currency's central bank surprises (yen, summer 2024).
  19. A $10 tariff lands on a $100 product built from a $50 import. Name the three ways it can be absorbed, and say why April 2025 broke a market rule. Foreign margin, US importer margin, or the consumer price. Stocks, Treasuries and the dollar fell together, so the "risk-free" asset behaved like a risk asset; the market was pricing US policy credibility.
  20. The reciprocal tariff on a country with $200 of US imports and $100 of US exports? (200 − 100) / 200 = 50%, halved to 25% (floor 10%). It measures the bilateral goods deficit, not the country's own tariffs, and ignores services.
  21. Why do Fed cuts move mortgage payments less today than in 2006? Almost no outstanding mortgages float (Patton: under 1% vs ~35% pre-GFC), most borrowers are locked in below market, and only ~10% of a mortgage's rate sensitivity sits on the 30-year point, while long yields can rise even as the Fed cuts (Sep 2024).
